(i) 2-Chloro-3-methylpentane — a five-carbon chain with \(\text{Cl}\) on C-2 and \(\text{CH}_3\) on C-3:
\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{Cl})\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3\)

(ii) 1-Chloro-4-ethylcyclohexane — a cyclohexane ring carrying \(\text{Cl}\) at C-1 and \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\) at C-4 (the two groups para across the ring):
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_{10}(\text{Cl})(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)\)

(iii) 4-tert. Butyl-3-iodoheptane — a seven-carbon chain with \(\text{I}\) on C-3 and \(-\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)_3\) on C-4:
\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}(\text{I})\text{CH}[\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)_3]\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3\)

(iv) 1,4-Dibromobut-2-ene — a four-carbon chain with the double bond between C-2 and C-3 and \(\text{Br}\) at each end:
\(\text{BrCH}_2\text{CH}=\text{CHCH}_2\text{Br}\)

(v) 1-Bromo-4-sec. butyl-2-methylbenzene — a benzene ring carrying \(\text{Br}\) at C-1, \(\text{CH}_3\) at C-2 and the sec-butyl group \(-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3\) at C-4.

Because sulphuric acid is an oxidising agent and destroys the very reagent the reaction needs.

The purpose of the acid is to liberate \(\text{HI}\) from \(\text{KI}\), which then converts the alcohol into the alkyl iodide:
\(\text{KI} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{KHSO}_4 + \text{HI}\)

But \(\text{HI}\) is a strong reducing agent, and concentrated \(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\) immediately oxidises it to iodine:
\(2\text{HI} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{I}_2 + \text{SO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}\)

So the \(\text{HI}\) is consumed as fast as it is formed and little alkyl iodide is obtained; sulphuric acid also dehydrates the alcohol to an alkene as a side reaction. A non-oxidising acid such as \(\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4\) is used instead.

Sulphuric acid is not used because it oxidises the \(\text{HI}\) produced to \(\text{I}_2\), so the alcohol is not converted to the iodide.

Propane has three carbons; replacing any two hydrogen atoms by halogen \(\text{X}\) gives four constitutionally different dihalides — two gem-dihalides (both halogens on one carbon) and two others:

\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHX}_2\) — 1,1-dihalopropane (gem)

\(\text{CH}_3\text{CHXCH}_2\text{X}\) — 1,2-dihalopropane (vic)

\(\text{XCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{X}\) — 1,3-dihalopropane

\(\text{CH}_3\text{CX}_2\text{CH}_3\) — 2,2-dihalopropane (gem)

Four dihalogen derivatives are possible.

There are three isomeric alkanes of formula \(\text{C}_5\text{H}_{12}\), and the number of monochlorides each gives is fixed by the number of DIFFERENT kinds of hydrogen it contains, since free-radical chlorination replaces each kind in turn.

(i) A single monochloride — 2,2-dimethylpropane (neopentane), \((\text{CH}_3)_4\text{C}\). All twelve hydrogen atoms belong to four equivalent methyl groups, so there is only one kind of hydrogen and only one product, \((\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CCH}_2\text{Cl}\).

(ii) Three isomeric monochlorides — pentane, \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3\). Its hydrogens are of three kinds (on C-1/C-5, on C-2/C-4 and on C-3), giving 1-chloropentane, 2-chloropentane and 3-chloropentane.

(iii) Four isomeric monochlorides — 2-methylbutane (isopentane), \((\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3\). Its hydrogens are of four kinds, giving 1-chloro-2-methylbutane, 2-chloro-2-methylbutane, 2-chloro-3-methylbutane and 1-chloro-3-methylbutane.

(i) Cyclohexanol with \(\text{SOCl}_2\) gives chlorocyclohexane; the \(-\text{OH}\) is replaced by \(-\text{Cl}\) and the by-products \(\text{SO}_2\) and \(\text{HCl}\) escape as gases.

(ii) \(\text{Br}_2\) with heat or UV light is free-radical (side-chain) substitution, not ring bromination, and it goes at the benzylic position because that radical is resonance-stabilised. The product is 1-(1-bromoethyl)-4-nitrobenzene, \(\text{O}_2\text{N}\text{C}_6\text{H}_4\text{CH}(\text{Br})\text{CH}_3\).

(iii) Only the alcoholic \(-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}\) reacts; the phenolic \(-\text{OH}\) is not replaced because its \(\text{C}-\text{O}\) bond has partial double-bond character from resonance with the ring. The product is 4-(chloromethyl)phenol, \(\text{HOC}_6\text{H}_4\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}\).

(iv) Addition of \(\text{HI}\) follows Markovnikov's rule, so \(\text{I}\) goes to the more substituted double-bond carbon (the one bearing the methyl group), which also gives the more stable tertiary carbocation. The product is 1-iodo-1-methylcyclohexane.

(v) \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Br} + \text{NaI} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{I} + \text{NaBr}\) — the Finkelstein halogen exchange, driven forward because \(\text{NaBr}\) is insoluble in dry acetone.

(vi) With heat and UV light bromine substitutes rather than adds, and it attacks the allylic position next to the double bond. The product is 3-bromocyclohexene.

Boiling point rises with molecular mass (stronger van der Waals forces) and falls with branching, because a branched molecule is more compact and has less surface contact.

(i) All four are halomethanes, so the order follows molecular mass: \(\text{CH}_3\text{Cl}\) (50.5), \(\text{CH}_3\text{Br}\) (95), \(\text{CH}_2\text{Br}_2\) (174), \(\text{CHBr}_3\) (253).
Chloromethane \(<\) Bromomethane \(<\) Dibromomethane \(<\) Bromoform.

(ii) Isopropyl chloride and 1-chloropropane are isomers, and the branched one boils lower; 1-chlorobutane has one carbon more than either and boils highest.
Isopropyl chloride \(<\) 1-Chloropropane \(<\) 1-Chlorobutane.

An \(\text{S}_\text{N}2\) reaction needs the nucleophile to reach the carbon from the side opposite the halogen, so the reaction is faster the less crowded that carbon is. Reactivity therefore falls in the order primary > secondary > tertiary.

(i) \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}\) reacts faster. It is a primary halide, whereas \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}(\text{Br})\text{CH}_3\) is secondary and carries an extra alkyl group beside the reaction centre.

(ii) \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}(\text{Br})\text{CH}_3\) reacts faster. It is secondary while \((\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CBr}\) is tertiary, and the three methyl groups of the latter block the backside approach almost completely.

(iii) \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}\) (1-bromo-3-methylbutane) reacts faster. Both compounds are primary, so the difference is where the branch sits: here it is on C-3, two carbons away from the reaction centre, whereas in \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{Br}\) it is on C-2, directly beside the carbon under attack, and hinders it.

An \(\text{S}_\text{N}1\) reaction is fastest when the carbocation formed in the slow step is most stable, and alkyl groups stabilise a carbocation by their electron-releasing inductive effect. Reactivity therefore rises in the order primary < secondary < tertiary.

(i) \((\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CCl}\) reacts faster. Losing chloride gives the tertiary \((\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}^+\) ion, which is stabilised by three alkyl groups, whereas 3-chloropentane can only give a secondary carbocation.

(ii) 2-Chloroheptane reacts faster. Its chlorine sits on C-2, so it gives a secondary carbocation, while 1-chlorohexane has its chlorine on a terminal carbon and would have to form a very unstable primary carbocation.

Each line is a Grignard reagent being made in dry ether and then destroyed by a proton (or deuteron) source, which converts \(\text{R}-\text{MgX}\) into \(\text{R}-\text{H}\) (or \(\text{R}-\text{D}\)).

Line 1: \(\text{A}\) is cyclohexylmagnesium bromide, \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_{11}\text{MgBr}\); water then protonates the carbanionic carbon, so \(\text{B}\) is cyclohexane, \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\).

Line 2: the product \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{D})\text{CH}_3\) carries the deuterium on the middle carbon, so that is the carbon that was bonded to magnesium. Hence \(\text{C}\) is isopropylmagnesium bromide, \((\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHMgBr}\), and \(\text{R}\) is the isopropyl group \((\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH}-\).

Line 3: with sodium in ether \(\text{R}^1-\text{X}\) undergoes Wurtz coupling, so the product 2,2,3,3-tetramethylbutane is simply two \(\text{R}^1\) units joined together. Cutting that molecule at its central bond gives \((\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}-\), so \(\text{R}^1\) is the tert-butyl group. Therefore \(\text{D}\) is tert-butylmagnesium halide, \((\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CMgX}\), and water converts it to \(\text{E}\), 2-methylpropane (isobutane), \((\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CH}\).

\(\text{A}\) = cyclohexylmagnesium bromide; \(\text{B}\) = cyclohexane; \(\text{C}\) = isopropylmagnesium bromide; \(\text{D}\) = tert-butylmagnesium halide; \(\text{E}\) = 2-methylpropane; \(\text{R}\) = isopropyl, \((\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH}-\); \(\text{R}^1\) = tert-butyl, \((\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}-\).
_note: The letter D does double duty in this question as printed: in line 2 it is a DEUTERIUM ATOM bonded to the middle carbon of the product (it comes from the \(\text{D}_2\text{O}\)), while in line 3 it is one of the unknown COMPOUNDS to be identified. The solution names both explicitly so the two cannot be confused.
